newRows.name: The Catholic Church in Africa in the Twentieth Century
newRows.region: Uganda, Rwanda, Zaire, Cameroon, sub-Saharan Africa
newRows.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1). It stands between the Africa and the Catholic lanes, because it belongs to both. Its window opens in 1906, where the entry on the Uganda Martyrs ends.
newRows.sourcing: Rich: two continental histories, by Adrian Hastings (1994) and by Bengt Sundkler and Christopher Steed (2000). The church's own dated texts run from 1956 to 1995.
newRows.floorNote: No question. It is the Catholic Church, which holds the Nicene Creed.
newRows.relationsSummary: It carries on the Catholic half of the Uganda Martyrs' story, which ends in 1906. Rome's own story in this era is told in the entries on the Catholic Church before and after the Second Vatican Council. The entry on the African-initiated churches tells of Africans who left the missions. This one tells of Africans who stayed in the Catholic Church.
newRows.why: In 1939 Pius XII consecrated Joseph Kiwanuka of Uganda as a bishop in Saint Peter's, Rome. He was the first sub-Saharan African made a Catholic bishop in the modern mission era. Thirty years later, at Kampala, Paul VI told Africa's bishops that they could, and must, have an African Christianity.

newRows.longDescription: On 25 May 1939 Joseph Kiwanuka was named vicar apostolic of Masaka, in Uganda. Pius XII consecrated him in Saint Peter's on 29 October that year. In 1956 a group of priests published Des prêtres noirs s'interrogent ('Black priests ask themselves questions'). Its writers included A. Abblé, A. Kagame, V. Mulago and M. Hebga. On 31 July 1969 Paul VI closed a symposium of Africa's bishops at Kampala. In his homily he told them they could, and must, have an African Christianity. In Zaire a trial text of the Mass came into use in 1974. Rome approved the Roman Missal for the Dioceses of Zaire on 30 April 1988, and Cardinal Joseph-Albert Malula was its chief promoter. In Katanga, in the Belgian Congo, the Franciscan Placide Tempels began the Jamaa movement. Its name is Swahili for 'family', and Johannes Fabian studied it in 1971 as a charismatic movement. In Rwanda the churches lived through the genocide of 1994. Timothy Longman argued that the churches had aligned with the state, and that church leaders backed the genocide to protect their own power. His thesis is contested. A special assembly of the Synod of Bishops for Africa met in Rome from 10 April to 8 May 1994. John Paul II signed its closing exhortation, Ecclesia in Africa, at Yaoundé on 14 September 1995.
newRows.teaser: Africa, 1906 to 2010 — the Catholic Church from Joseph Kiwanuka's consecration in 1939 to the African Synod of 1994. Its story includes a missal for Zaire and the hard question of Rwanda.

newRows.longDescription: This story opens with the Cottesloe Consultation, which met in Johannesburg from 7 to 14 December 1960. In September 1985 a group who called themselves the Kairos Theologians issued the Kairos Document. It was made public on 25 September. Its full title called it a theological comment on the political crisis in South Africa. The number of people who signed it differs from one edition to another. In October 1982 a synod of the Dutch Reformed Mission Church, meeting at Belhar, accepted a draft confession. The church adopted it as a confession in 1986. Its first article confesses the triune God, who through his Word and Spirit gathers, protects and cares for his church. The movement ended with apartheid in 1994.

newRows.longDescription: Roland Werner, William Anderson and Andrew Wheeler wrote the standard history, Day of Devastation, Day of Contentment (2000). It runs to 688 pages and covers the Sudanese church across two thousand years. Marc Nikkel studied the conversion of the Dinka people in Dinka Christianity (2001). The war that began in 1983 ended with the peace agreement of 9 January 2005. Jesse Zink has told how many Dinka people embraced Anglican faith in that war.

newRows.longDescription: In Mexico the Calles Law took effect on 31 July 1926. That day the bishops suspended public worship. Catholics of the National League for the Defense of Religious Liberty, founded in March 1925, took up arms. So did rural fighters called cristeros. The settlement of June 1929, the arreglos, brought an amnesty and the non-enforcement of the law. Jean Meyer told the war's history in the three volumes of La Cristiada (1973-74). On 21 May 2000 John Paul II canonized 25 of its martyrs, Cristóbal Magallanes and his companions. From 25 July to 4 August 1955 Latin America's bishops held their first General Conference, at Rio de Janeiro. There they set up CELAM, their continental council, under Pius XII. Its seat was in Bogotá. Its first president was Cardinal Jaime de Barros Câmara. The second General Conference met at Medellín, Colombia, in August and September 1968. Its document read the church's task in Latin America in the light of the Council. One chapter was titled 'Poverty of the Church'. The third General Conference met at Puebla, Mexico, in 1979. Leonidas Proaño was bishop of Riobamba, Ecuador, from 1954 to 1985. He came to Riobamba on 29 May 1954 and retired on 29 January 1985. Under him, projects for Indigenous people opened in Chimborazo province. One was the Centro de Estudios y Acción Social ('Center for Social Studies and Action'), in 1960. The Escuelas Radiofónicas Populares del Ecuador ('Popular Radio Schools of Ecuador') began on 19 March 1962. Latin American scholars began to write this church's history themselves. One group of them, CEHILA, was founded in 1973 under Enrique Dussel. From 1981 it published a general history of the church in Latin America.
newRows.teaser: Latin America, 1906 to 2010 — the Catholic Church of the Cristero War and of CELAM. Its bishops met as one continent at Rio, Medellín and Puebla.

newRows.region: Panama, Guatemala, Colombia, Bolivia, Peru, Mexico
newRows.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window opens with the Panama congress of 1916. Its dated acts are the congresses and councils the churches held together.

newRows.longDescription: The Panama congress met from 10 to 20 February 1916. A committee formed in 1913 organized it. It drew 304 delegates and visitors from 21 nations. Few of them were Latin Americans. Its reports came out in three volumes in 1917. In November 1969 the first Latin American Congress on Evangelization, called CLADE, met in Bogotá. In 1970 the Latin American Theological Fraternity met for the first time, at Cochabamba in Bolivia. Churches met at Huampaní in Peru in 1977 and at Oaxtepec in Mexico in 1978. They meant to form a council of their own. That council, CLAI, was set up at Huampaní in 1982. One source gives 1983. A more conservative body, CONELA, formed as its alternative. Virginia Garrard-Burnett found that Protestants in Guatemala won few converts until the 1960s. Then military power and violence spread. They weakened people's old ties. Indigenous evangelicals in Ecuador organized themselves too. Julián Guamán is an Indigenous author from Ecuador. He dates the start of that organizing to Chimborazo in 1966. The national council of these evangelicals, FEINE, was founded in 1980. Guamán counts more than 1,500 local congregations among them. Susana Andrade studied why Indigenous people in Chimborazo became Protestants. Her book of 2004 sets out to show how Pentecostalism there took on a Quichua form. It took back themes from Indigenous religion. The themes include prayer, the interpretation of dreams and baptism in lagoons.
newRows.teaser: Latin America, 1916 to 2010 — Protestant churches that met at Panama in 1916 and then built councils of their own. Evangelical faith grew fast in Guatemala.

newRows.longDescription: On 17 September 1907 the first presbytery of an independent Presbyterian Church in Korea met. Its 78 members were 38 missionaries and 40 Korean elders. It ordained seven Korean pastors, that year's graduates of the seminary in Pyongyang. It also took up the Twelve Articles of Faith, at first for a year of study. The articles came from the Presbyterian Church in India, which had drawn them up in 1904. In 1938 the Pyongyang seminary was shut down, because it had opposed the shrine worship that Japan enforced. In the 1950s the Presbyterian church divided into several churches, among them Kosin, Kijang, Hapdong and Tonghap. Kijang separated in 1953 over its progressive theology, especially its view of Scripture. Timothy Lee's Born Again (2010) tells the century as a story of evangelicalism in Korea.
newRows.teaser: Korea's Protestants, from their first presbytery in 1907 through Japanese rule and the church divisions of the 1950s.

newRows.longDescription: In wartime, the Kyodan later wrote, the government demanded that religious bodies unite and cooperate with the war effort. Most Japanese Protestants had long wanted a single evangelical church. Their leaders used the demand to enter a church union, and the Kyodan was formed. It marked its twenty-fifth anniversary in October 1966. On 26 October 1954 its Eighth General Assembly enacted a Confession of Faith. It called the Bible "the unerring standard of faith and life", and it confessed the Apostles' Creed. On Easter Sunday, 26 March 1967, its moderator, Suzuki Masahisa, issued a confession on the church's wartime responsibility. The church, it said, "should not have aligned itself with that war effort". It asked forgiveness from the peoples of Asia and from their churches. Beside the Kyodan grew Japan's own Christian movements, which Mark Mullins studied in Christianity Made in Japan (1998).

newRows.longDescription: On 12 September 1920, at Sremski Karlovci, the Serbian Orthodox Church was declared united. Constantinople recognized it in a Tomos, a formal decree, dated 19 February 1922. Its first patriarch was Dimitrije. Sources differ on the date of his election. In Romania the Holy Synod voted for a patriarchate on 4 February 1925. A law followed on 25 February. A Tomos from Constantinople followed on 30 July. Miron Cristea was enthroned as the first patriarch on 1 November 1925. In 1945 the schism between the Bulgarian church and Constantinople was lifted. On 10 May 1953 a church-people's council restored the Bulgarian patriarchate. It elected Kiril of Plovdiv. In Bucharest a prayer movement called the Burning Bush met at the Antim monastery from about 1945. It was outlawed in 1948. Its members were arrested in June 1958 and tried that November. Among them were Sandu Tudor, later Father Daniil, Benedict Ghiuș and Sofian Boghiu.
newRows.teaser: Romania, Bulgaria, Serbia and Albania, 1920 to 2010 — the Balkan Orthodox churches under communist rule. Three of them became patriarchates between 1920 and 1953.
